prompt: After the second push in this lesson, `cosign verify` against `linkbox:main` fails while the commit's tag passes. Why?

choices.text: Pushing under a tag deletes every signature stored in that repository
choices.why: The commit's tag still verified after the push, so its signature was still there.

choices.text: cosign compares the tag with the tag name recorded at signing time
choices.why: cosign resolves the tag to a digest and checks the digest; the signed document names no tag.

choices.text: main now names a digest that nobody signed
choices.why: Right. The signature belongs to the first digest and stayed with it; the tag moved away.

choices.text: The registry flags a moved tag as untrusted until someone approves it
choices.why: The registry keeps no record of where a tag pointed before, so it has nothing to flag.

prompt: `sha256sum` of the index the registry served printed exactly the `Docker-Content-Digest` header. What does that property give a client?

choices.text: A way to tell who built the image
choices.why: A hash says which bytes, not who made them. Anybody can compute it, including whoever pushed the image.

choices.text: A check that the bytes it received are the bytes it asked for by digest
choices.why: Right. If a registry served other bytes under that digest, the client's own hash would disagree.

choices.text: A guarantee that the tag will keep pointing at these bytes
choices.why: The tag moved in the very next capture; a digest says nothing about tags.

choices.text: Proof that a scanner has read the image
choices.why: No scanner is involved in computing a digest.

prompt: A registry answers a `HEAD` request for a manifest with its hash in the ___ header.
Why does this course sign with a signing config that lists no services?

choices.text: Without it, cosign refuses to sign images held in a registry on localhost
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson shows such a refusal; the reason is what the default would publish, and that the services cannot be reached here.

choices.text: An empty config lets the signature verify without any public key
choices.why: Verification still needs `cosign.pub`, as every capture shows.

choices.text: It removes the need for the password on `cosign.key`
choices.why: The password is still read from `COSIGN_PASSWORD` for every signature.

choices.text: The default records each signature in Rekor, a public log
choices.why: Right: it would publish the digests and the name of a private registry, and the recording machine cannot reach Rekor anyway.

prompt: Of the four files in `~/ci/keys`, which two together can sign anything in the CI's name?

choices.text: `cosign.key` and `cosign.pub`
choices.why: Without the password the private key cannot be decrypted, and the public key cannot sign.

choices.text: `cosign.key` and `password`
choices.why: Right. The private key is encrypted with that password; either alone is not enough.

choices.text: `password` and `offline.json`
choices.why: `offline.json` only lists services, here none; it holds no key.

choices.text: `cosign.pub` and `offline.json`
choices.why: Neither holds anything secret; together they can verify, not sign.

prompt: Which statements are true of the signature `cosign sign` pushed by hand in this lesson? Choose every one that is.

choices.text: It sits in the same registry, under a tag named after the digest
choices.why: Right: the tag list showed `sha256-` followed by the digest.

choices.text: It was recorded in Rekor, Sigstore's public log
choices.why: The signing config listed no log, and the machine cannot reach Rekor.

choices.text: What it signed names the image's digest, not its tag
choices.why: Right: the verified JSON carries `docker-manifest-digest` and no tag.

choices.text: A second registry had to be set up to hold it
choices.why: The registry of lesson 8 held it with no new feature.

prompt: Verifying the moved tag `main` printed `no signatures found`. What exit status did `cosign verify` return?
A teammate pushes an image and, beside it in the same registry, a `cosign.pub` of their own. Verification against that key passes. What is wrong with the check?

choices.text: Nothing: the signature is valid, so the image may be deployed
choices.why: It is valid for a key anybody could have made. A signature is only as good as the trust in its key.

choices.text: The verifier took its key from a place the image's author controls
choices.why: Right. Whoever can push an image can push a key beside it; the key must come from where only the CI's is published.

choices.text: Two public keys in one registry make every signature in it invalid
choices.why: Signatures are checked against the key you pass; other keys nearby change nothing.

choices.text: The image should have been verified by tag instead of by digest
choices.why: Verifying by tag still checks a digest; the trouble is which key was trusted.

prompt: A deployment runs `cosign verify` on `linkbox:main` at 10:00, and at 10:01 runs `docker pull linkbox:main`. What can go wrong?

choices.text: By 10:01 the tag names whatever was pushed last, verified or not
choices.why: Right. What was verified is a digest; pull that digest instead of the tag.

choices.text: The signature expires a few seconds after it is verified
choices.why: A key-pair signature has no such expiry; the problem is the tag.

choices.text: `docker pull` cannot read an image that cosign has signed already
choices.why: The CI's own `docker pull` of a signed digest worked in this lesson.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as both commands run on the same machine
choices.why: Where the commands run does not stop somebody else moving the tag in the registry.

prompt: Why is `sign` the last entry in `ci/stages`?

choices.text: cosign has to run after the tests because it imports the project's code
choices.why: cosign reads the registry, not linkbox's code.

choices.text: A signature then means every stage before it passed
choices.why: Right. The pipeline stops at the first failure, so signing last turns the signature into a statement that the image went through the whole list.

choices.text: Signing first would make the build stage slower
choices.why: Order is about meaning, not speed; signing took seconds.

choices.text: The image has no digest until the sbom stage has run
choices.why: The digest exists from the push; the bill of materials is needed only for one attestation.

prompt: The key and its password live in `~/ci/keys`, outside every clone of linkbox. Which risk does that arrangement leave in place?

choices.text: A fork of linkbox carries the key to whoever forks it
choices.why: That is exactly what keeping it out of the repository prevents.

choices.text: A leaked backup of the git history exposes the password
choices.why: The history never held it, so a backup of it cannot leak it.

choices.text: A pushed branch changes `ci/sign.sh` and uses the key in its own run
choices.why: Right. The hook runs the stage scripts of the pushed commit, so the commit decides what happens to the key.

choices.text: Verifiers cannot reach `cosign.pub` from another machine
choices.why: Publishing the public key is a separate step; it is meant to be everywhere.

prompt: Put the steps of `ci/sign.sh` in the order the script runs them.
items: find the digest the push recorded
write the provenance beside the logs

prompt: Match each field of an in-toto statement to what it holds.

pairs.right: the artefact, named by its digest
what kind of claim the statement makes

right_distractors: the public key that verifies it

prompt: `cosign verify-attestation` with `~/hosted.cue` exits 1 with `conflicting values`. What did it find?

choices.text: The attestation's signature did not match `cosign.pub`
choices.why: The signature checks passed and were listed; the failure came after, from the policy.

choices.text: The image carried no provenance attestation at all, so there was nothing to read
choices.why: Without one it would say no attestation matched the type; here it read the predicate and compared a field.

choices.text: The builder id in the provenance is not the one the policy demands
choices.why: Right. The signed statement says the laptop's hook built it, and the policy accepts only another builder.

choices.text: CUE cannot read a predicate written by a Python program
choices.why: The first policy read the same predicate and passed.

prompt: `docker build` already adds an `attestation-manifest` to the image index. What does the pipeline's own provenance add?

choices.text: A signature by the CI's key over the statement
choices.why: Right. Docker's statement is written by the builder and signed by nobody; this one is vouched for by the CI.

choices.text: The list of packages installed in the image
choices.why: That is the bill of materials, a separate attestation.

choices.text: A proof that the image has no known vulnerabilities
choices.why: Provenance says how something was built, never whether it is free of flaws.

choices.text: Build L3, because the provenance is now signed
choices.why: Signing alone does not climb past L1 here; the builder is a laptop and the build's steps can read the key.

prompt: Which SLSA Build level does this course's pipeline meet?

choices.text: Build L3: the provenance is signed and stored in the registry
choices.why: L3 needs the signing key out of reach of the build's steps, and `ci/sign.sh` comes from the commit.

choices.text: Build L2: a CI server writes and signs the provenance
choices.why: The CI server is a hook on the developer's own laptop, not a hosted build platform.

choices.text: Build L1: provenance exists for every image
choices.why: Right. It has the shape of L2, a signature, without the hosted platform that gives it substance.

choices.text: Build L0: provenance written by a script does not count
choices.why: A script writing provenance is exactly what L1 asks; who writes and signs it decides the higher levels.

prompt: In keyless signing, what does Fulcio do?

choices.text: Records every signature in a public, append-only log
choices.why: That is Rekor, the transparency log.

choices.text: Exchanges an OIDC token for a certificate valid for ten minutes
choices.why: Right: it binds a fresh key pair to the identity the token names.

choices.text: Stores the CI's long-lived private key and signs every image on its behalf
choices.why: No long-lived key exists in keyless signing; the fresh key is thrown away after one use.

choices.text: Checks the image for vulnerabilities before it is signed
choices.why: Fulcio never sees the image's contents; it issues certificates.

prompt: Why can lesson 10's ValidatingAdmissionPolicy not require a cosign signature?

choices.text: CEL has no way to compare strings with a public key
choices.why: The limit is not string handling; the signature is somewhere the rule cannot read.

choices.text: Its rules read only the object being admitted and cannot fetch from a registry
choices.why: Right. A signature lives in the registry, so the check needs a controller that asks for it.

choices.text: Kubernetes refuses any image that carries an attestation
choices.why: Kubernetes ignores the extra tags; pods ran from attested images in this course.

choices.text: Admission policies run after the pod has started
choices.why: Admission runs before the object is stored, which is its whole point.

prompt: A release script runs `cosign verify` on `localhost:5000/linkbox@sha256:…` and then applies a manifest that names `localhost:5000/linkbox:main`. Which single change closes the gap?

choices.text: Verify `linkbox:main` instead, so the check uses the same name
choices.why: Then both steps use a tag, which can move between them; the gap is still there.

choices.text: Sign the image a second time just before the apply
choices.why: Another signature of the same digest says nothing about what the tag points at.

choices.text: Add a CUE policy that checks the builder id
choices.why: Useful, but it checks the verified digest too, and the manifest still deploys a tag.

choices.text: Put the verified digest in the manifest instead of the tag
choices.why: Right. What runs is then exactly what was checked.

prompt: To save CI time, a colleague proposes that reviewers sign images on their own laptops after approving a merge. What does a signature stop meaning?

choices.text: That the signer is a member of the team
choices.why: It would still mean that; a reviewer is on the team. What it loses is the link to the pipeline.

choices.text: That the image went through the pipeline
choices.why: Right. A key on many laptops says 'somebody approved', not 'this passed the list'.

choices.text: That the image's digest matches its manifest
choices.why: That is arithmetic, true of any digest whoever signs.

choices.text: That the signature was recorded in a public log
choices.why: No signature in this course is, by design.
